input.text: Reviewing a final year thesis that allegedly contains uncredited passages from published papers
input.criteria: Evaluate academic integrity and originality

why: Academic plagiarism cases are judged by professors, academics, or academic integrity boards.

input.text: Assessing the ecological damage and cleanup efforts following a coastal crude oil spill
input.criteria: Evaluate environmental impact and remediation effectiveness

why: Oil spill evaluation requires specific scientific expertise in environmental impact.

input.text: Investigating an international syndicate laundering money through decentralized finance protocols
input.criteria: Evaluate regulatory violations and blockchain transaction traceability

why: Cross-border crypto fraud requires both legal/financial regulation expertise and technical blockchain knowledge.

input.text: Investigating an outbreak of E. coli linked to a local restaurant chain's produce supplier
input.criteria: Evaluate health code compliance and contamination source

why: Food safety violations specifically require health inspectors or food safety experts.

input.text: Evaluating a factory worker's claim of chronic back pain resulting from repetitive lifting
input.criteria: Evaluate occupational hazard and workplace safety protocols

why: Ergonomic injuries require specialists in occupational health or ergonomics.

input.text: Determining liability in a multi-vehicle crash caused by an autonomous taxi turning left
input.criteria: Evaluate technical fault and legal liability

why: Liability for an autonomous-vehicle crash needs technical knowledge of autonomous systems (an automotive engineer or AI expert).

input.text: Analyzing a new microchip architecture for potential infringement on existing US patents
input.criteria: Evaluate intellectual property boundaries and technical overlap

why: Patent infringement of a chip requires legal IP experts and hardware engineers.

input.text: Reviewing patient records to determine if surgical protocol was followed correctly
input.criteria: Evaluate medical procedure and standard of care

why: A medical malpractice jury requires a medical professional to establish the standard of care.

input.text: {"ticket_id":"TCK-88102","customer_tier":"Enterprise","description":"Production database connection pool exhausted during payment gateway callback webhook. Customers receiving 500 errors on checkout page.","recent_logs":"ERROR PoolExhaustedException: Connection timeout waiting for connection from pool of 50 connections.","impact":"High revenue impact ($10k/min lost sales)"}
input.criteria: Identify expert technical roles needed to conduct incident post-mortem and evaluate system recovery actions.

why: A DB connection pool exhaustion incident puts database expertise first, and recovery needs SRE/infrastructure expertise somewhere in the list.

input.text: Evaluating a new machine learning resume screener that disproportionately rejects female candidates
input.criteria: Evaluate algorithmic fairness and ethical implications

why: Evaluating AI bias requires ML experts or ethicists to understand the algorithmic and societal impacts.

input.text: SPRING MENU - Mains. Pan-roasted hake, wild garlic butter, crushed new potatoes (F, D). Satay chicken skewers, cucumber relish, jasmine rice (G). Wild mushroom risotto, aged parmesan, truffle oil (V, D). Thai green curry with king prawns and coconut rice (Cr). Allergen key: F fish, D dairy, G gluten, Cr crustaceans, V vegetarian. Please tell your server about any allergies before ordering.
input.criteria: Evaluate whether the allergen labelling is complete and accurate under food allergen labelling rules.

why: The criteria ask about allergen labelling, not the food, so the juries are food safety, allergen or labelling-compliance people (the satay is missing peanuts, the curry fish sauce and the risotto possibly celery). A food critic, blogger or sommelier knows the dishes but cannot judge allergen compliance. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: Internal safety report 24-117. During the ILS approach to runway 27L the aircraft was 25 kt above Vref and high on the glideslope at 1,000 ft AGL. The crew continued, citing a tailwind that was expected to drop off, and initiated a go-around at 300 ft when the stabilised approach criteria were still not met. Root cause: late descent clearance from ATC. Corrective action: remind crews of the stabilised approach policy by bulletin.
input.criteria: Evaluate whether the report identifies the real root causes and proposes effective corrective actions.

why: Judging root causes of an unstable approach needs aviation safety or flight operations expertise: an airline captain or training pilot, an aviation safety investigator, a human factors specialist. Passengers, cabin crew or marketing have no say on approach discipline. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: Charming 2-bed, 1-bath bungalow in quiet Maple Heights. Hardwood floors throughout, renovated kitchen with quartz counters, fenced backyard. Perfect for young professionals or a mature couple; not suited to families with kids. Walking distance to St. Mary's church and the country club. $2,150/month, no Section 8. Call Linda to book a viewing.
input.criteria: Evaluate whether the listing complies with fair housing advertising rules and avoids discriminatory language.

why: The criteria are about discrimination in advertising (familial status, religion, source of income), so the juries are a fair housing compliance specialist, a real estate or civil rights attorney, a housing regulator. An interior designer, stager or photographer would judge the home, not the wording. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: Package leaflet: information for the patient. Take one 5 mg tablet twice a day, about 12 hours apart, with or without food. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember and continue twice daily; do not take a double dose. This medicine increases the risk of bleeding. Seek urgent help if you notice black stools, blood in your urine, coughing up blood, or a severe headache. Tell your dentist or surgeon you take this medicine before any procedure.
input.criteria: Evaluate whether a patient with no medical background can understand the dosing instructions and the bleeding-risk warnings.

why: Two things are judged: whether the medical content is right (a pharmacist or physician) and whether a layperson understands it (a health literacy or plain-language specialist, or a patient representative). Drug sales, marketing or a medicinal chemist know the molecule, not the reader. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: Opening five minutes of a stand-up set, written in the style of George Carlin and Dave Chappelle: "They call it a 'smart' fridge. My fridge knows I'm out of milk, but it doesn't know I'm out of money. Last week it ordered oat milk on my card. I don't even like oats. That's not smart, that's a roommate with my PIN..." The bit then moves to self-checkout machines, 'unexpected item in the bagging area', and ends on a callback to the fridge.
input.criteria: Evaluate the set's comedic timing, originality and use of callbacks.

why: Timing and callbacks are judged by comedy professionals: a stand-up comedian, a comedy writer, a comedy club booker or comedy critic. The text names Carlin and Chappelle, which invites using famous comedians as juries; the prompt asks for job titles, never people's names. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: Rear deck, 4.8 m x 3.6 m, attached to the house with a ledger board. Joists 45x190 C24 at 600 mm centres, span 3.6 m. Design imposed load 1.5 kN/m2 as for a domestic floor, dead load 0.5 kN/m2. Ledger fixed with M10 coach screws at 600 mm into the rim joist. Posts 100x100 on concrete pads 400x400x300. Deflection checked at span/250: OK.
input.criteria: Evaluate whether the load calculation is correct and the design meets building code requirements.

why: Checking loads, spans and ledger fixings against the code is work for a structural engineer, a building inspector or building control officer, perhaps an experienced deck builder. A landscape or garden designer knows decks as features of a garden, but not their load paths. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: Manuscript, ages 3-5. 'Pip the hedgehog could not find his scarf. He looked under the toadstool. Not there! He looked behind the big brown log. Not there! The wind went whoosh. Pip felt cold and a little bit sad. Then Owl flew down. "Is this yours?" she hooted. It was Pip's scarf! Owl had found it in her tree. Pip said thank you and gave Owl a hug, a careful hug, because of his prickles.'
input.criteria: Evaluate whether the story's vocabulary and themes are appropriate for children aged 3 to 5.

why: Vocabulary and themes for ages 3-5 are judged by an early childhood educator, a child development specialist, a children's librarian or a picture book editor. An illustrator or art director judges the art, and a wildlife expert the hedgehog, not the words. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: Module 3: Spot the phish. Phishing emails often have spelling mistakes, generic greetings like 'Dear Customer', and come from strange addresses. If an email looks professional and comes from a colleague's real address, it is safe to open its attachments. Hover over links to see where they go. Never give your password over email. Quiz: Which is a phishing email? (a) an email with typos asking for your bank details (b) your manager asking you to review a shared document.
input.criteria: Evaluate whether the training teaches employees to recognise the phishing techniques attackers use today.

why: Whether a module reflects real phishing (compromised colleague accounts, polished lures) is judged by security people: a security awareness lead, a red teamer or social engineer, a threat analyst, perhaps an instructional designer. A copywriter or designer judges the presentation, and payroll is only a target. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: Drought-year irrigation schedule, 40 ha almond orchard, Central Valley, sandy loam. Water allocation cut to 60% of normal. Plan: keep full irrigation through bloom and kernel fill (March-June), regulated deficit irrigation at 50% ETc during hull split (July), then 40% ETc post-harvest until leaf drop. Drip lines checked monthly for clogging; soil moisture probes at 30 and 60 cm in four blocks.
input.criteria: Evaluate the plan's water efficiency and its risk to this year's and next year's crop yield.

why: Deficit irrigation and yield risk are judged by an agronomist or crop scientist, an irrigation engineer or hydrologist, and an experienced almond grower or extension advisor. A chef or nutritionist knows almonds as food, which has nothing to do with the criteria. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: Original (pt-BR): "Cláusula 9ª - O LOCATÁRIO não poderá sublocar, ceder ou emprestar o imóvel, no todo ou em parte, sem o prévio consentimento por escrito do LOCADOR, sob pena de rescisão contratual e multa equivalente a três aluguéis." Translation (en): "Clause 9 - The TENANT may not sublet, assign or lend the property, in whole or in part, without the prior written consent of the LANDLORD, under penalty of contract termination and a fine equivalent to three months' rent."
input.criteria: Evaluate the translation's fidelity to the legal meaning of the original clause.

why: Legal fidelity needs both languages and the law: a sworn or legal translator, and a lawyer who knows Brazilian lease law (a bilingual contract lawyer covers both). A realtor or property manager uses leases but cannot judge a translation's legal equivalence. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: 12-week plan for a first marathon, for a runner who currently runs 15 km a week. Week 1: 30 km. Week 2: 40 km. Weeks 3-8: add 8 km a week, long run growing from 18 km to 35 km. Weeks 9-11: 85 km a week, two 35 km long runs. Week 12: race. Speed work every Tuesday from week 1. Rest days optional; push through minor pain, it is part of the process.
input.criteria: Evaluate the plan's injury risk and whether its mileage progression is safe for a first-time marathoner.

why: Injury risk and mileage progression are judged by a running coach, a sports medicine physician or physiotherapist, an exercise physiologist. Race directors and sports journalists know marathons but not training load, and a nutritionist is outside these criteria. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: Customer: "My ceramic lamp arrived smashed. Third broken order this year. I want a refund, not another replacement." Agent reply: "Hi Sam, I'm really sorry, that's frustrating, especially after the earlier orders. I've issued a full refund to your card, you'll see it in 3-5 working days. You don't need to send the lamp back; please recycle it safely. I've also flagged your account so future fragile items ship double-boxed."
input.criteria: Evaluate the reply's empathy and tone, and whether it resolves the customer's issue under the store's return policy.

why: A support reply is judged by customer experience people: a CX or support team lead, a quality assurance analyst for support, a returns policy owner. The broken lamp invites logistics, packaging or ceramics experts, but they cannot judge tone or policy. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: Council briefing: a GBP 8 daily charge for private cars entering the inner ring road, 7am-7pm on weekdays. We assume a 20% fall in car trips, all of it shifting to buses, which have spare capacity. Revenue of GBP 45m a year after running costs is ring-fenced for bus priority lanes. Retail footfall is not expected to change, as most shoppers already arrive by bus. Emissions in the zone fall by an estimated 15%.
input.criteria: Evaluate the brief's economic assumptions and its expected effect on traffic.

why: The criteria are economics and traffic, so the juries are a transport economist, a traffic engineer or transport planner, perhaps a public finance economist. The emissions line invites a climate scientist, but climate science cannot test the demand or revenue assumptions. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: Gallery 4, case 12. Silver denarius of the Emperor Hadrian, minted in Rome around AD 134-138. The reverse shows the goddess Roma seated, holding Victory. Coins like this paid a legionary's daily wage and circulated across the empire, from Britain to Syria. Found in a hoard of 212 coins near Hexham, Northumberland, in 1998.
input.criteria: Evaluate the historical accuracy of the museum label.

why: Historical accuracy of a Roman coin label is judged by a numismatist, a historian of Rome, an archaeologist or a curator of antiquities. A jeweller, an auction house or a designer would judge its metal, its price or its layout. The prompt asks for three juries.

input.text: We're hiring a Rockstar Full-Stack Ninja! Join our young, energetic team of digital natives in our beer-on-tap office. You're a recent grad (2022 or later) who can hit the ground running, work hard and play hard, and isn't afraid of 60-hour weeks during launches. Must be a culture fit. Stack: React, Node, Postgres. Competitive salary, ping-pong, free snacks.
input.criteria: Evaluate whether the job posting uses inclusive language and avoids age or gender bias.

why: Inclusive language and age bias are judged by a DEI specialist, an HR or recruiting lead, an employment lawyer. The posting is for a developer, which invites a software engineer as a jury, but the criteria are about bias in the wording, not the tech stack. The prompt asks for three juries.
